decision.quote: Crutchfield [ 8 ] studied the effect of intellectual competence on conformity. He found that higher competence was associated with lower levels of conformity. However, intelligence was measured by the subjective ratings of the experimental staff. Iscoe, Williams, and Harvey [ 10 ] exposed high school students (7 to 15 years) to group pressure in an acoustic task (counting metronome ticks), and approximated intelligence by subjects’ school records. They found no correlation of school records with conformity. Uchida et al. [ 31 ] studied 12 to 14 year-old high school students and assessed scholastic achievements by their school performance. They report that high achievers conformed less to the majority than low achievers. Hence, results of the effect of intelligence on conformity are inconclusive so far and the existing studies use indirect measures (school grades) but do not measure intelligence directly.
decision.reason: In Section 2.3 (line 109), the authors review Iscoe, Williams, and Harvey (1964) [10] as finding no correlation between intelligence approximated via school records and conformity in 7- to 15-year-old children in an acoustic metronome task, calling prior evidence on intelligence and conformity inconclusive to motivate H5 (line 111) and their adult Hagen Matrices Test (HMT) fluid-intelligence regression (Section 4, lines 153, 164). However, they simultaneously critique existing studies as using 'indirect measures (school grades)' rather than measuring intelligence directly, do not collect school records or test children on an acoustic task, and never compare their HMT results back to Iscoe et al. [10] in Results or Discussion. As established in conformity_trait_originals_0086, the primary full text and abstract of Iscoe et al. (1964) remain unavailable after bounded attempts, leaving the original's exact school-record construct and tested contrasts unverified beyond this secondary description. Because the available primary evidence cannot resolve whether the current adult HMT regression conceptually retests a specific finding of Iscoe et al. (1964), the target is undeterminable.

decision.reason: Although Section 2.3 (line 109) cites Uchida, Michael, and Mori (2020) [31] in the intelligence review preceding H5 (line 111), the full primary text of Uchida et al. (2020) inspected in conformity_trait_originals_0086 establishes that the original study did not measure IQ or cognitive intelligence at all: it classified 12- to 14-year-old junior high school students into low/middle/high scholastic achievement tertiles using five-subject regular term exam scores and manipulated peer-group majority/minority achievement-status combinations (HHLH, HHHH, LLHL, LLLL) in a no-confederate fMORI paradigm as a test of peer social status and confidence. Consistent with the current authors' explicit distinction that existing studies 'use indirect measures (school grades) but do not measure intelligence directly,' the current experiment measures individual adult fluid intelligence via the 6-item Hagen Matrices Test (HMT) in a 5-confederate task without measuring academic achievement or peer-status group compositions and never compares its results to Uchida et al. [31] in Results or Discussion. Thus, Uchida et al. (2020) is not an empirically retested target.

decision.quote: The effect of self-esteem (or self-assertiveness, self-consciousness) on conformity was only investigated in a few studies so far. Kurosawa [ 11 ] found no effect on conformity when the decision of the minority subject was preceded by two confederates. In groups of four, confederates’ self-esteem had a negative effect on conformity. Similarly, Tainaka et al. [ 32 ] found in a sample of Japanese female students that those with low self-esteem conformed more often in a co-witness task.
decision.reason: Section 2.3 (line 110) reviews Kurosawa (1993) [11] (10.4992/jjpsy.63.379) directly before formulating H6 (negative association between participant self-esteem and conformity, line 111), but literally states that Kurosawa found 'no effect on conformity when the decision of the minority subject was preceded by two confederates' and that '[i]n groups of four, confederates’ self-esteem had a negative effect on conformity.' As shown in conformity_trait_originals_0086, Kurosawa's primary English abstract (full Japanese article body unavailable) actually reports an interaction of pressure level (four vs. two preceding others) with public self-consciousness and an independent negative effect of the respondent's own self-esteem under high pressure (four others) but a null effect under low pressure (two others). Meanwhile, the current study uses a fixed 5-confederate group, tests only the naive participant's Rosenberg self-esteem main effect (lines 153, 164), and never cites Kurosawa [11] in Results or Discussion. Without repairing the current text's literal confederate/participant misattribution or accessing the unavailable Japanese full body, empirical retest correspondence remains undeterminable.

Tainaka et al. (2014) has no printed DOI in the reference list (line 225) and is completely distinct from shipped row 6 (Asch 1956, 10.1037/h0093718) and all sibling targets.

counterpart of English most (povečeto in Bg, większość in Pl, henceforth Most1) and a closely
